stimuli.title: Passage 1: the village pond
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

For a long time the standard story about shared resources was a gloomy one. A pasture, a fishery or a village pond that everyone may use, the argument ran, will be used by everyone until it is ruined, because each user gains the whole benefit of taking a little more while the cost of the damage is spread across all. The cure, on this view, had to come from outside: either the state takes charge and rations the resource, or the resource is divided into private plots whose owners have a reason to look after them.

The trouble with the story is that it describes a situation that is rarer than it sounds. It assumes users who cannot talk to one another, cannot watch one another and will never meet again. Real villages are nothing like this. The families who draw water from a pond have usually done so for generations; they know who takes what, and they will have to live beside each other next year. Under those conditions people have repeatedly worked out their own rules: turns for irrigation, closed seasons for fishing, fines for the household that grazes too many goats, and a council to settle quarrels.

Such arrangements are not romantic. They work only when certain conditions hold. The boundaries of the resource and the list of rightful users must be clear. The people who bear the rules must have a hand in making them, or the rules will be resented and evaded. Breaches must be noticed cheaply, often by the users themselves rather than by a paid guard, and punishments should start small and grow, so that a first offence is a warning rather than a disaster. Above all, outside authorities must leave the arrangement room to breathe.

That last condition is where well-meant reform has often done harm. When a distant department declares a forest or a lake to be state property and posts a single officer to guard it, the old rules lose their force overnight, while the officer cannot possibly watch every path. What was a commons governed by its users becomes, in practice, a resource open to anyone. The lesson is not that the state has no role, but that it should strengthen the local institutions that already exist instead of replacing them with a fence it cannot maintain.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: what a measurement is
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

We tend to think of a measurement as a window: the instrument shows us a number that was sitting in the world, waiting to be read. A thermometer reports the temperature; a scale reports the weight. On this picture, better instruments simply give us clearer windows, and the history of science is the history of polishing the glass.

The picture is not wrong so much as incomplete. Consider what had to be settled before anyone could measure temperature at all. Early instrument makers built tubes of coloured spirit that rose and fell with warmth, but two such tubes made in different workshops would disagree, and there was no obvious way to decide which was right. To calibrate a thermometer one needs fixed points, conditions that always produce the same degree of heat, and one needs to know that the liquid expands evenly between them. Yet the only way to check that the liquid expands evenly is to compare it with a thermometer one already trusts. The makers were caught in a circle.

They escaped it not by proof but by a slow process of mutual adjustment. Fixed points were proposed, tested against one another and discarded when they proved unreliable. Different liquids were compared, and instruments that agreed with many others were preferred to those that agreed with few. No single step was justified from outside the system; the system as a whole became trustworthy because it hung together better and better.

This matters beyond the history of thermometers. If measurement rests on a web of agreed procedures, then a number is never merely read off the world. It is the product of choices that a community has made and could, in principle, make differently. That is not a reason for doubt. A web that has been tested from many directions is far stronger than any single strand. But it does mean that when two instruments disagree, the question of which one is right cannot always be settled by looking harder at the world. Sometimes it has to be settled by asking which procedures we have the best reasons to keep.

stimuli.title: Passage 3: the translator's choices
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Every translator of poetry eventually meets the same complaint: the translation is not the poem. The complaint is true and useless. Of course a poem written in one language cannot be reproduced in another; its sounds belong to its words, and its words belong to a way of speaking that has its own history. The interesting question is not whether something is lost but what the translator chooses to keep.

Broadly, there are two loyalties. The first is to the sense of the original, line by line, so that a reader who knows both languages could lay the versions side by side and find nothing added and nothing left out. Translations made this way are honest and often dull. They report what the poem says while losing what it does, much as a summary of a joke reports the joke without being funny.

The second loyalty is to the effect. A translator of this school asks what the poem did to its first readers, how it surprised, consoled or disturbed them, and then tries to produce that experience in the new language, even if this means changing images, rearranging lines or replacing a reference that a foreign reader would not catch. Translations made this way can be alive in a way the first kind rarely are, but they carry a risk. The more freely the translator works, the more the result reflects the translator's own taste, and the reader cannot easily tell where the poet ends and the translator begins.

Most good translators move between these loyalties from line to line rather than choosing one for good. A pun may be impossible to keep and must be sacrificed for sense; a rhythm may matter more than any single word and must be kept at the cost of a word. What readers should ask of a translation, then, is not fidelity in the abstract but candour: a willingness to tell the reader, in a note or a preface, which losses were accepted and why. A reader who knows the bargain can trust the work even where it departs from the original.

stimuli.title: Passage 4: why animals sleep
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Sleep is a strange thing for an animal to do. For hours at a time the sleeper stops eating, stops watching for danger and stops looking for a mate. Any trait that costs so much should, one might think, have been trimmed away by natural selection unless it pays for itself handsomely. Yet nearly every animal that biologists have looked at closely shows some form of sleep or a resting state much like it, from mammals and birds to fish and insects.

The breadth of the habit has encouraged a search for a single purpose. Some researchers stress the brain: sleep, they argue, is when connections made during the day are sorted, the useful strengthened and the trivial weakened. Others point to the body as a whole, suggesting that sleep is a time of repair, when energy that would otherwise go to movement and alertness can be spent on maintenance. Still others treat sleep chiefly as a way of keeping an animal still and quiet during the hours when it would gain little and risk much by being active.

These explanations are usually presented as rivals, but there is little reason why they must be. A trait that has existed for a very long time can pick up new uses along the way, just as a building put up for one purpose may later house several. Sleep may have begun as a cheap way of lying low and acquired other jobs because a resting brain and body made those jobs easier to do.

If that is right, the search for the purpose of sleep may be partly misdirected. Different animals could rely on sleep for different things, and the balance could shift with age, so that what sleep does for a growing young animal is not what it does for an adult. The more useful question may be not why sleep exists but what each particular animal would lose if it went without.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: who the street is for
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Ask a city planner how a street is performing and you will often be shown a count of vehicles: how many pass a junction each hour and how long they wait at the lights. These numbers are easy to collect and easy to compare, and a road that moves more vehicles faster is said to be working better. The trouble is not that the numbers are wrong but that they quietly decide whom the street is for.

A street is also where people walk to the bus stop, where children cross on their way to school, where a vendor sets up a cart and where neighbours stop to talk. None of these activities shows up in a traffic count, and several of them are made harder by the measures that improve it. Widening a road to move cars faster lengthens the crossing for a pedestrian. Removing a cart to clear a lane removes a reason to walk there at all.

Planners are not villains for relying on vehicle counts. What gets measured gets attention, and walking has long been treated as something people do anyway, needing no help. In many growing cities, however, most trips are still made on foot or by public transport, at least for part of the way. A street designed around the minority who drive serves the majority poorly, and the cost falls hardest on those with the fewest alternatives.

Some cities have begun to count differently, measuring how long it takes to cross a road on foot, how far apart safe crossings are, and how many people use a street rather than how many vehicles pass through it. These measures are harder to gather and they produce awkward conclusions, such as that a slower road can be a better one. But a street judged only by its throughput will keep being rebuilt for throughput, and the people it was never counting will keep finding it harder to use.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: rules and improvisation
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

To a listener hearing it for the first time, improvised music can sound like freedom itself: the performer simply plays whatever comes to mind. Musicians who improvise tell a different story. The freedom they value is not the absence of rules but the ability to move fluently within them, and that fluency is built through years of disciplined practice.

In many traditions an improviser works inside a frame that the listener may not notice. A melodic mode supplies the notes that may be used and suggests which of them carry weight. A rhythmic cycle sets how long a phrase may run before it must return to its starting point. Within such a frame the performer has enormous room to invent, but the invention is heard against the frame, and much of its pleasure comes from the way it stretches the frame without breaking it. A phrase that seems to wander away and then lands exactly on the first beat of the cycle delights the audience precisely because they knew where it had to land.

This is why improvisation is so hard to teach by explanation alone. A student can learn the rules of a mode in an afternoon, but knowing the rules is not the same as being able to think in them at speed. The teacher's task is to make the rules so familiar that the student stops consulting them, much as a fluent speaker no longer consults grammar while talking.

Seen this way, the contrast between composed and improvised music is less sharp than it appears. A composer chooses notes slowly and can revise; an improviser chooses quickly and cannot. Both, however, are making choices against a background of expectations they share with their listeners. What differs is the time available for the choice, not whether the choice is constrained.

stimuli.title: Passage 3: maps and their makers
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A map is often praised for its accuracy, as if the best map were simply the one that matched the ground most closely. But a map that matched the ground in every detail would be as large as the ground and just as hard to use. Every useful map leaves things out, and what it leaves out reflects the purposes of the person who drew it.

A sailor's chart marks depths, rocks and lighthouses and pays little attention to towns a mile inland. A tax surveyor's map records boundaries between fields with great care and may ignore the paths people actually walk. Neither is wrong; each answers a different question. The danger arises when a map made for one purpose is taken as a neutral picture of the world and used for another.

History offers many examples of this danger. Maps drawn by administrators to count land and collect revenue sometimes recorded a single owner for land that in practice was used by many families under shared customs. When later officials read these maps as statements of fact, the shared uses vanished from the record, and with them the claims of the people who depended on them. The map did not merely describe a situation; it helped to create one.

None of this means that maps cannot be trusted. It means that a reader should ask of any map who made it, for what, and what it would have been easy or convenient for its maker to leave out. Those questions do not make a map less useful. They make it possible to use it for what it is good at without mistaking it for a picture of everything.

stimuli.title: Passage 4: the reading room
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

When information became cheap to reach, many people predicted that libraries would fade away. Why travel to a building to consult a book when the same text, or something like it, can be found on a phone in seconds? The prediction has proved only half right. Libraries have lent fewer of some kinds of books, yet in many towns their reading rooms are fuller than ever.

The explanation lies in what was actually scarce. A generation ago the scarce thing was access: the book you needed might exist only on a particular shelf. Today access is plentiful and attention is scarce. A phone offers every text at once, along with a stream of messages, alerts and invitations to look at something else. The value of a reading room now lies less in what it holds than in what it keeps out.

Students preparing for examinations understand this well. Many of them have the same material at home, yet they queue for a seat in a public library because a quiet room full of other people working makes it easier to keep working. The room supplies a kind of shared discipline that is hard to produce alone.

If this account is right, libraries that measure their success only by the number of books lent are counting the wrong thing. A library that lends fewer books but gives hundreds of people a few hours of undistracted work each day may be doing more good than ever. The building, it turns out, was never only a container for books. It was also a place that made a certain kind of attention possible, and that has become rarer and more precious.

stimuli.title: Passage: notes and memory
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Students are often told that taking notes helps them remember, and the advice is usually right, but not always for the reason given. Notes are commonly thought of as a store: you write things down so that you can look them up later. That is one use, and a valuable one. The less obvious use is that the act of writing a note, if done well, forces the writer to decide what matters.

A student who copies a lecture word for word, as some do when they type quickly, gains a complete record and very little understanding. Nothing has been chosen, compressed or connected; the words have passed from ear to fingers without much stopping in between. A student who writes slowly cannot copy everything and must summarise, and summarising is a form of thinking. To put an idea in fewer words, you have to know what the idea is.

This is why some teachers warn against laptops in lectures, though the warning can be overstated. The problem is not the machine but the habit it encourages. A student with a laptop who deliberately writes in their own words, and only the points worth keeping, gains the same benefit as one with a pen. A student with a pen who copies the slides gains nothing.

The deeper point is that memory is not mainly a matter of storage. We remember what we have worked on. Notes help when they are a record of that work, and harm when they let us believe the work has been done because the words are safely on the page.

stimuli.title: Passage: the craftsman and the machine
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Whenever a machine learns to do a task that people used to do by hand, two predictions follow. One says the craft will disappear, as the hand weaver gave way to the power loom. The other says that the craft will survive as a luxury, prized because it is made by hand. Both predictions contain some truth, but they share a mistaken assumption: that the craft is the same thing as the task the machine has taken over.

A craft is rarely a single task. A carpenter cuts and joins wood, but she also judges which piece of timber will warp, talks a customer out of a design that will not last, and repairs work that a careless builder left behind. When a machine takes over the cutting, the cutting becomes cheap, but the judgement becomes, if anything, more important, because there is now more cut wood in the world and more ways for it to be badly used.

This is why the effect of automation on a trade is so hard to forecast from a list of its tasks. The tasks that machines take over are usually the ones that are easiest to describe, and those are often not the ones that made the worker valuable. The parts of a craft that resist description, knowing when something is about to go wrong, or what a client really wants, tend to remain.

None of this guarantees that every worker will be better off. A trade whose valuable judgement can be exercised by a few people while machines do the rest may need far fewer hands. But it suggests that the question to ask of any new machine is not only what it can do, but what doing that cheaply will make more necessary.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
options: Village councils are usually more corrupt than the government departments above them
Shared resources are always ruined unless the state takes direct control of them
Dividing a commons into private plots is the most reliable way to protect it
Users of a shared resource can often govern it themselves under the right conditions
questions.explanation: The passage rejects the gloomy standard story and argues that users who know one another have repeatedly made their own rules, provided certain conditions hold. It never says private plots are best or that councils are corrupt.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the standard story about shared resources assumes that users:
options: always prefer private ownership to any form of shared use
cannot talk to, watch or meet one another again
know exactly how much of the resource each family has taken
are willing to pay a guard to watch over the resource for them
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the story "assumes users who cannot talk to one another, cannot watch one another and will never meet again." Knowing what each family takes is the opposite, a feature of real villages.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that a fine of the full value of a season's catch for a first breach of a fishing rule would be:
options: unnecessary, because breaches are never noticed by users
acceptable only if the state rather than the users set it
a poor design, because penalties should start small and rise
a sound design, because it deters every user equally
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says punishments "should start small and grow, so that a first offence is a warning rather than a disaster." A ruinous first fine breaks that condition.

questions.stem: What does the author suggest the role of the state should be in managing a commons?
options: Support the local institutions that already govern it
Withdraw entirely and leave all disputes to the courts
Take ownership and post officers to guard the resource
Divide the resource among the families who use it
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the lesson "is not that the state has no role, but that it should strengthen the local institutions that already exist". Withdrawing entirely goes further than the author does.

questions.stem: The author's main purpose in the passage is to:
options: argue that early thermometers were too unreliable to be of any scientific use
explain the chemistry that makes some liquids expand more evenly than others
prove that every measurement is a matter of opinion and cannot be trusted
show that measurement depends on agreed procedures, not just on instruments
questions.explanation: The passage uses the history of the thermometer to argue that a number is "the product of choices that a community has made". The author explicitly says this is "not a reason for doubt", which rules out the claim that measurement cannot be trusted.

questions.stem: The "circle" in which the early thermometer makers were caught was that:
options: fixed points could only be found by using a calibrated scale
each workshop refused to compare its tubes with another's
checking even expansion needed a trusted thermometer
coloured spirit froze at the very points they wished to test
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the only way to check that the liquid expands evenly "is to compare it with a thermometer one already trusts". That is the circle.

questions.stem: The way the makers escaped the circle is most similar to:
options: a judge who settles a dispute by appealing to a written law
a crossword trusted because its answers fit together
a map maker who copies the boundaries from an older map
a student who checks a sum by looking at the answer key
questions.explanation: The makers escaped through mutual adjustment: the system "became trustworthy because it hung together better and better", with no single step justified from outside. A crossword's answers support each other the same way; an answer key or a written law is an outside authority.

questions.stem: Which statement about two disagreeing instruments is supported by the passage?
options: Deciding between them may require judging which procedures to keep
The newer of the two instruments should always be preferred
Looking more closely at the world will always reveal the right one
Disagreement shows that both instruments are badly made
questions.explanation: The final sentences say the question "cannot always be settled by looking harder at the world" and sometimes means "asking which procedures we have the best reasons to keep".

questions.stem: The passage is chiefly concerned with:
options: what a translator chooses to keep from a poem
the history of how translation became a profession
a comparison of two well-known translations of one poem
the reasons poetry should never be translated at all
questions.explanation: After dismissing the complaint that a translation is not the poem, the author says the interesting question is "what the translator chooses to keep" and examines the two loyalties.

questions.stem: The author calls the complaint that "the translation is not the poem" true and useless because:
options: most readers cannot read the original language anyway
the complaint is made only by poets about their own work
the loss is unavoidable, so the real issue is what is kept
translators have already answered it in their prefaces
questions.explanation: The complaint is true because sounds and words cannot be carried over, and useless because loss is certain; the author turns at once to "what the translator chooses to keep."

questions.stem: The comparison with a summary of a joke is used to show that a sense-for-sense translation can:
options: make a serious poem sound light-hearted to the reader
add jokes and puns that the original poet never wrote
be funnier than the poem it sets out to translate
report what a poem says while losing what it does
questions.explanation: The passage says such translations "report what the poem says while losing what it does, much as a summary of a joke reports the joke without being funny."

questions.stem: Which quality does the author most want readers to look for in a translation?
options: Strict fidelity to the sense of each original line
Openness about which losses were accepted and why
Preservation of the poet's rhyme and metre at any cost
Freedom to reshape the poem to suit modern taste
questions.explanation: The last paragraph asks not for "fidelity in the abstract but candour: a willingness to tell the reader ... which losses were accepted and why."

questions.stem: Why does the author call sleep "a strange thing for an animal to do"?
options: Sleeping animals use more energy than waking ones
It is hard to tell when an insect is actually asleep
It gives up feeding, vigilance and mating for hours
Only a small number of animal groups sleep at all
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the sleeper "stops eating, stops watching for danger and stops looking for a mate", a large cost. The passage says nearly every animal studied sleeps, so sleep is not rare.

questions.stem: The central claim of the third paragraph is that:
options: buildings are a better model for evolution than animals
sleep began as a way of repairing the body after effort
the brain-sorting theory of sleep has been disproved
the proposed functions of sleep need not exclude one another
questions.explanation: The paragraph says the explanations "are usually presented as rivals, but there is little reason why they must be", since a long-lived trait can pick up new uses.

questions.stem: The comparison with a building is meant to suggest that sleep:
options: may have gained new functions after it first evolved
is too complex for any one scientist to understand
will eventually be abandoned once it stops being useful
was designed for a single purpose that it still serves
questions.explanation: A building "put up for one purpose may later house several"; likewise sleep "may have begun as a cheap way of lying low and acquired other jobs".

questions.stem: Which question does the author consider more useful than asking for the purpose of sleep?
options: Whether sleep evolved before or after animals had brains
What a particular animal would lose by not sleeping
How many hours of sleep each species needs per day
Which animal group was the first to begin sleeping
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the more useful question may be "what each particular animal would lose if it went without."

questions.stem:
The four sentences below, labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4, form a coherent paragraph when put in the right order. Decide the order and type it as a sequence of four numbers (for example, 2143).

1. Much of the work, however, is done by a large crew whose names appear only in the closing credits.

2. Audiences tend to credit a film's success to its director and its stars.

3. Without these specialists the director's vision would remain an idea on paper.

4. This crew includes editors, sound designers and set builders, who shape much of what we finally see and hear.
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 opens with the common view. Sentence 1 turns against it with "however" and introduces the crew. Sentence 4 names the crew's specialists, and sentence 3 refers back to them as "these specialists". Order: 2143.

questions.stem:
The four sentences below, labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4, form a coherent paragraph when put in the right order. Decide the order and type it as a sequence of four numbers (for example, 2143).

1. Once the moisture has gone, the leaves are rolled to break their cells and release their juices.

2. Fresh tea leaves are first spread out in a warm room and allowed to wilt.

3. Finally they are heated to stop the oxidation at the point the maker wants.

4. The released juices react with the air, darkening the leaves and deepening the flavour.
questions.explanation: The process runs in sequence: wilting (2), rolling once the moisture has gone (1), the released juices reacting with air (4), and heating "finally" to stop the reaction (3). Order: 2143.

The four sentences below, labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4, form a coherent paragraph when put in the right order. Decide the order and type it as a sequence of four numbers (for example, 2143).

1. This is why a sudden fall in prices worries policymakers more than a mild rise.

2. When prices are expected to fall, people delay their purchases in the hope of paying less later.

3. Firms that sell less then cut wages or jobs, which lowers spending further.

4. The delay itself reduces sales today.
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 sets up the expectation, 4 gives its first effect ("the delay itself"), 3 continues the chain (firms that sell less), and 1 draws the conclusion with "This is why". Order: 2431.

questions.stem:
Five sentences about a topic are given below, labelled 1 to 5. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not fit and type its number.

1. Coral reefs cover a very small share of the ocean floor.

2. Yet they shelter a remarkably large share of the sea's species.

3. Many fish breed in reefs before moving to open water as adults.

4. Deep-sea trenches are among the least explored places on Earth.

5. Damage to a reef can therefore be felt far beyond the reef itself.
questions.explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 build one argument about reefs: small in area, rich in species, nurseries for open-water fish, so their damage spreads. Sentence 4 about deep-sea trenches does not belong.

questions.stem:
Five sentences about a topic are given below, labelled 1 to 5. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not fit and type its number.

1. A good apprenticeship teaches more than the skills of a trade.

2. The apprentice also learns how experienced workers judge quality and solve problems.

3. Many of these judgements are never written down in any manual.

4. Some trades now require a written examination before a licence is granted.

5. They are passed on through years of working side by side.
questions.explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 explain how unwritten judgement passes from master to apprentice; "they" in sentence 5 refers to the judgements in sentence 3. Sentence 4 about licensing examinations is off the point.

questions.stem:
The passage below is followed by four summaries. Choose the one that best captures the essence of the passage.

"Many people assume that a forest left alone will always return to what it was before it was disturbed. In practice, the forest that grows back depends on what is left behind. If the soil has washed away, or if the seeds of the original trees are no longer nearby, a different kind of forest, or no forest at all, may take its place."
options: Soil erosion is the main reason forests fail to recover after logging.
Forests left alone always return to their original state after a disturbance.
Whether a forest recovers depends on what survives the disturbance.
Seeds of the original trees can travel long distances to restart a forest.
questions.explanation: The passage corrects the assumption that a forest always returns: what grows back depends on the soil and seeds left behind. Soil erosion is one example, not "the main reason".

questions.stem:
The passage below is followed by four summaries. Choose the one that best captures the essence of the passage.

"A rule that is never enforced does more than fail to achieve its purpose. It teaches people that rules in general need not be taken seriously, and that lesson spreads to rules that are enforced. An organisation with many dead rules on its books may therefore find it harder to secure obedience to the few that matter."
options: Unenforced rules weaken respect for every rule, including important ones.
People obey rules only when they fear the penalty for breaking them.
Rules that are never enforced simply fail to achieve their purpose.
Organisations should enforce every rule strictly, however minor it is.
questions.explanation: The passage's point is that a dead rule teaches disrespect for rules in general, which spreads to the rules that matter. Simple failure of purpose is what it says the harm goes beyond.

questions.stem:
The passage below is followed by four summaries. Choose the one that best captures the essence of the passage.

"Early photographs often show empty streets in busy cities. This was not because the streets were empty but because exposures took so long that anyone moving did not register. Only a person who stood still, such as a man having his boots polished, might appear. The pictures are accurate records of what the camera could see, not of what was there."
options: Photographers posed people in the street to make their pictures livelier.
City streets were much quieter in the early days of photography.
Early cameras were more accurate than the painters they replaced.
Early photographs record only what slow exposures could catch.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that long exposures erased moving people, so the photographs record what the camera could see. It denies that the streets were actually empty.

questions.stem: What were the total sales of Gamma for the whole year, in Rs lakh?
In which quarter did the company's total sales grow by the highest percentage over the previous quarter?
options: Q4
Q2
Q3 and Q4 equally
Q3
questions.explanation: Quarterly totals are 160, 180, 200 and 210. Growth is 20/160 = 12.5% in Q2, 20/180 = 11.1% in Q3 and 10/200 = 5% in Q4. The same rise of 20 is a bigger share of the smaller base, so Q2 leads.

questions.stem: What percentage of the company's total sales in Q3 came from Gamma?
Which product's sales rose by the greatest percentage from Q1 to Q4?
options: Delta
Alpha
Beta
Gamma
questions.explanation: Beta 36 to 51 is +41.7%, Alpha 48 to 64 is +33.3%, Gamma 30 to 39 is +30% and Delta 46 to 56 is +21.7%. Alpha has the largest rise in lakh (16) but not in percentage.

questions.stem: How many employees use exactly one of the three apps?
questions.explanation: Mail and Chat only = 70 - 20 = 50, Mail and Video only = 30, Chat and Video only = 20. Mail only = 160 - 50 - 30 - 20 = 60, Chat only = 140 - 50 - 20 - 20 = 50, Video only = 100 - 30 - 20 - 20 = 30. Exactly one = 60 + 50 + 30 = 140.

questions.stem: How many employees use none of the three apps?
questions.explanation: Those using at least one app = 60 + 50 + 30 (one app) + 50 + 30 + 20 (two apps) + 20 (all three) = 260, so 300 - 260 = 40 use none.

questions.stem: How many employees use exactly two of the apps?
questions.explanation: Subtract those using all three from each pair: (70 - 20) + (50 - 20) + (40 - 20) = 50 + 30 + 20 = 100. Adding the pair totals without removing the 20 who use all three gives 160, which counts those 20 three times over.

questions.stem: How many employees use Chat but not Mail?
questions.explanation: Chat users who do not use Mail are Chat only (50) plus Chat and Video only (20) = 70. Equivalently, 140 Chat users minus the 70 who also use Mail.

questions.stem: Who sits opposite Chirag?
options: Bela
Divya
Esha
Farhan
questions.explanation: Number the seats clockwise from Arjun (seat 0). Bela is opposite, in seat 3, and Chirag is in seat 1. Farhan cannot be in seat 5, next to Arjun, and Divya cannot be in seat 2, next to Chirag, so Divya is in seat 5. Esha must sit next to Bela but not next to Divya, so Esha is in seat 2 and Farhan in seat 4. Seat 4, opposite Chirag's seat 1, is Farhan's.

questions.stem: Who are Divya's two neighbours?
options: Arjun and Farhan
Arjun and Chirag
Bela and Farhan
Esha and Bela
questions.explanation: Number the seats clockwise from Arjun (seat 0). Bela is opposite, in seat 3, and Chirag is in seat 1. Farhan cannot be in seat 5, next to Arjun, and Divya cannot be in seat 2, next to Chirag, so Divya is in seat 5. Esha must sit next to Bela but not next to Divya, so Esha is in seat 2 and Farhan in seat 4. Divya in seat 5 sits between Farhan (seat 4) and Arjun (seat 0).

questions.stem: Counting clockwise from Arjun, how many people sit between Arjun and Esha?
questions.explanation: Number the seats clockwise from Arjun (seat 0). Bela is opposite, in seat 3, and Chirag is in seat 1. Farhan cannot be in seat 5, next to Arjun, and Divya cannot be in seat 2, next to Chirag, so Divya is in seat 5. Esha must sit next to Bela but not next to Divya, so Esha is in seat 2 and Farhan in seat 4. Going clockwise from Arjun (seat 0) to Esha (seat 2), only Chirag (seat 1) is passed.

questions.stem: Who sits between Esha and Farhan?
options: Arjun
Divya
Bela
Chirag
questions.explanation: Number the seats clockwise from Arjun (seat 0). Bela is opposite, in seat 3, and Chirag is in seat 1. Farhan cannot be in seat 5, next to Arjun, and Divya cannot be in seat 2, next to Chirag, so Divya is in seat 5. Esha must sit next to Bela but not next to Divya, so Esha is in seat 2 and Farhan in seat 4. Esha is in seat 2 and Farhan in seat 4, so Bela in seat 3 sits between them.

questions.stem: On which day is the Strategy talk held?
options: Wednesday
Tuesday
Monday
Thursday
questions.explanation: Strategy follows Finance and is on neither Thursday nor Friday, so the pair is Monday-Tuesday or Tuesday-Wednesday; Operations comes before Finance, so it is Operations Monday, Finance Tuesday, Strategy Wednesday. Marketing cannot be Wednesday and must come before HR, so Marketing is Thursday and HR Friday. Strategy is on Wednesday.

questions.stem: How many talks are held between the Operations talk and the HR talk?
questions.explanation: Strategy follows Finance and is on neither Thursday nor Friday, so the pair is Monday-Tuesday or Tuesday-Wednesday; Operations comes before Finance, so it is Operations Monday, Finance Tuesday, Strategy Wednesday. Marketing cannot be Wednesday and must come before HR, so Marketing is Thursday and HR Friday. Operations is Monday and HR Friday; Finance, Strategy and Marketing fall between them.

questions.stem: Which talk is held on Thursday?
options: HR
Finance
Strategy
Marketing
questions.explanation: Strategy follows Finance and is on neither Thursday nor Friday, so the pair is Monday-Tuesday or Tuesday-Wednesday; Operations comes before Finance, so it is Operations Monday, Finance Tuesday, Strategy Wednesday. Marketing cannot be Wednesday and must come before HR, so Marketing is Thursday and HR Friday. Thursday is Marketing.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
options: Finance is held on Thursday
Operations is held on Wednesday
HR is the last talk of the week
Marketing is held on Tuesday
questions.explanation: Strategy follows Finance and is on neither Thursday nor Friday, so the pair is Monday-Tuesday or Tuesday-Wednesday; Operations comes before Finance, so it is Operations Monday, Finance Tuesday, Strategy Wednesday. Marketing cannot be Wednesday and must come before HR, so Marketing is Thursday and HR Friday. HR on Friday is the last talk; the other three statements contradict the schedule.

questions.stem: How many points did Mynas finish with?
questions.explanation: Orioles lost all three matches, so each other team beat them. Larks beat Mynas, so the single draw was Kestrels against Larks or Kestrels against Mynas. If Kestrels drew with Larks, both would have 5 points, which the no-tie rule forbids. So Kestrels drew with Mynas and beat Larks: Kestrels 5, Larks 4, Mynas 3, Orioles 0. Mynas drew with Kestrels (1) and beat Orioles (2): 3 points.

questions.stem: Which match was drawn?
options: Kestrels v Larks
Kestrels v Mynas
Mynas v Orioles
Larks v Mynas
questions.explanation: Orioles lost all three matches, so each other team beat them. Larks beat Mynas, so the single draw was Kestrels against Larks or Kestrels against Mynas. If Kestrels drew with Larks, both would have 5 points, which the no-tie rule forbids. So Kestrels drew with Mynas and beat Larks: Kestrels 5, Larks 4, Mynas 3, Orioles 0.

questions.stem: How many matches did Larks win?
questions.explanation: Orioles lost all three matches, so each other team beat them. Larks beat Mynas, so the single draw was Kestrels against Larks or Kestrels against Mynas. If Kestrels drew with Larks, both would have 5 points, which the no-tie rule forbids. So Kestrels drew with Mynas and beat Larks: Kestrels 5, Larks 4, Mynas 3, Orioles 0. Larks beat Mynas and Orioles and lost to Kestrels: two wins.

questions.stem: What was the result of the match between Kestrels and Larks?
options: It was drawn
It cannot be determined
Larks won
Kestrels won
questions.explanation: Orioles lost all three matches, so each other team beat them. Larks beat Mynas, so the single draw was Kestrels against Larks or Kestrels against Mynas. If Kestrels drew with Larks, both would have 5 points, which the no-tie rule forbids. So Kestrels drew with Mynas and beat Larks: Kestrels 5, Larks 4, Mynas 3, Orioles 0. A draw between them would leave Kestrels and Larks level on 5 points, so Kestrels must have won.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above its cost price and then gives a discount of 15% on the marked price. What is his profit as a percentage of the cost price?
questions.explanation: If the cost is 100, the marked price is 140 and the selling price is 85% of 140 = 119, a profit of 19%. Subtracting 15 from 40 (25%) ignores that the discount is taken on the higher marked price.

questions.stem: A 60-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. How many litres of water must be added to make the ratio 3 : 2?
questions.explanation: The mixture has 45 litres of milk and 15 of water. For milk : water = 3 : 2 the water must be 30 litres, so 15 litres are added.

questions.stem: A can finish a job in 18 days and B in 27 days. They work together for 6 days, then A leaves and B finishes the job alone. How many days does the job take in all?
questions.explanation: Together they do 1/18 + 1/27 = 5/54 of the job a day, so 6 days complete 30/54 = 5/9. B does the remaining 4/9 at 1/27 a day in 12 days, so the job takes 6 + 12 = 18 days.

questions.stem: A 240-metre train passes completely over a 360-metre platform in 30 seconds. What is its speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: The train covers its own length plus the platform, 600 m, in 30 s: 20 m/s. Multiply by 18/5 to get 72 km/h. Using only the platform's length gives 12 m/s, about 43 km/h.

questions.stem: What is the compound interest, in rupees, on Rs 20,000 for 2 years at 9% a year, compounded annually?
questions.explanation: Amount = 20,000 x 1.09 x 1.09 = 23,762, so the interest is 23,762 - 20,000 = 3,762. Simple interest would be only 3,600; the extra 162 is interest on the first year's interest.

questions.stem: The average age of 30 students is 15 years. When the teacher's age is included, the average rises to 16 years. What is the teacher's age in years?
questions.explanation: The 31 ages total 31 x 16 = 496 and the students' ages total 30 x 15 = 450, so the teacher is 496 - 450 = 46.

questions.stem: The price of sugar rises by 25%. By what percentage must a family cut its consumption to keep its spending on sugar unchanged?
questions.explanation: Spending = price x quantity. If the price becomes 5/4 of the old price, quantity must become 4/5, a cut of 1/5 = 20%. Cutting by 25% would reduce spending.

questions.stem: A invests Rs 40,000 for 12 months and B invests Rs 60,000 for 8 months in a business. Out of a profit of Rs 36,000, what is A's share?
questions.explanation: Shares follow money x time: 40,000 x 12 = 4,80,000 and 60,000 x 8 = 4,80,000, a ratio of 1 : 1, so A gets half, Rs 18,000. Splitting by the amounts alone (2 : 3) gives Rs 14,400.

questions.stem: If $a$ and $b$ are the roots of $x^2 - 7x + 10 = 0$, what is the value of $a^2 + b^2$?
questions.explanation: The roots sum to 7 and multiply to 10, so $a^2 + b^2 = (a + b)^2 - 2ab = 49 - 20 = 29$. Directly, the roots are 2 and 5, and 4 + 25 = 29.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = 3x + 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$, what is $f(g(2))$?
questions.explanation: $g(2) = 4 + 1 = 5$, and $f(5) = 15 + 2 = 17$. Applying the functions in the other order, $g(f(2)) = g(8) = 65$.

questions.stem: If $3x + 2y = 24$ and $x - y = 3$, what is the value of $xy$?
questions.explanation: From the second equation $x = y + 3$. Substituting, $3y + 9 + 2y = 24$, so $y = 3$ and $x = 6$. Then $xy = 18$.

questions.stem: The 5th term of an arithmetic progression is 17 and its 12th term is 38. What is the sum of its first 20 terms?
questions.explanation: Seven steps raise the term by 21, so the common difference is 3 and the first term is 17 - 12 = 5. The 20th term is 5 + 57 = 62, and the sum is 20/2 x (5 + 62) = 670.

questions.stem: What is the sum to infinity of the series 18 + 6 + 2 + ... ?
questions.explanation: The common ratio is 1/3, so the sum is 18 / (1 - 1/3) = 18 x 3/2 = 27.

questions.stem: How many integers $x$ satisfy $|x - 4| < 6$?
questions.explanation: $|x - 4| < 6$ means $-6 < x - 4 < 6$, that is $-2 < x < 10$. The integers from -1 to 9 number 11. The end points -2 and 10 are excluded because the inequality is strict.

questions.stem: What is the value of $\log_2 8 + \log_3 81 - \log_5 25$?
questions.explanation: $\log_2 8 = 3$, $\log_3 81 = 4$ and $\log_5 25 = 2$, so the value is 3 + 4 - 2 = 5.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has legs of 9 cm and 12 cm. What is the length, in cm, of the perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse is 15 cm. The area is 9 x 12 / 2 = 54, and also hypotenuse x height / 2, so the height is 108/15 = 7.2 cm.

questions.stem: A circle has an area of 616 sq cm. Taking $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$, what is its circumference in cm?
questions.explanation: $\frac{22}{7} r^2 = 616$ gives $r^2 = 196$ and $r = 14$. The circumference is $2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 88$ cm.

questions.stem: A cube has a volume of 216 cubic cm. What is its total surface area in sq cm?
questions.explanation: The side is the cube root of 216, which is 6 cm. Total surface area = 6 x 6^2 = 216 sq cm. Four faces only (the lateral area) give 144.

questions.stem: What is the distance between the points (-1, 4) and (11, -1)?
questions.explanation: The differences are 12 and 5, so the distance is the square root of 144 + 25 = 169, which is 13.

questions.stem: What is the remainder when $2^{100}$ is divided by 7?
questions.explanation: $2^3 = 8$ leaves remainder 1 on division by 7. Since $2^{100} = (2^3)^{33} \times 2$, the remainder is $1 \times 2 = 2$.

questions.stem: How many positive factors does 360 have?
questions.explanation: $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$, so the number of factors is (3 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 24.

questions.stem: A committee of 3 is to be chosen from 6 men and 4 women. In how many ways can it be formed with exactly 2 women?
questions.explanation: Choose 2 of the 4 women in 6 ways and 1 of the 6 men in 6 ways: 6 x 6 = 36.

questions.stem: The main argument of the passage is that:
options: vehicle counts make streets serve drivers over others
traffic counts are too inaccurate to guide road design
planners deliberately ignore pedestrians to please car owners
street vendors are the main cause of congestion in cities
questions.explanation: The passage says vehicle counts "quietly decide whom the street is for" and that a street designed around drivers serves the walking majority poorly. It says planners "are not villains", so deliberate neglect is wrong.

questions.stem: According to the passage, widening a road to move cars faster:
options: makes the crossing longer for a person on foot
reduces the number of buses that use the street
attracts more vendors to set up carts on the street
shortens the waiting time for pedestrians at lights
questions.explanation: The second paragraph: "Widening a road to move cars faster lengthens the crossing for a pedestrian."

questions.stem: Why, according to the author, has walking received little attention from planners?
options: Pedestrians rarely complain about the streets they use
Most planners do not themselves walk in the city
Walking trips are too short to be worth measuring
It was assumed people would walk anyway without help
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says walking "has long been treated as something people do anyway, needing no help".

questions.stem: The author mentions that the new measures "produce awkward conclusions" in order to:
options: suggest that cities should return to vehicle counts
argue that slower roads always cause more accidents
show that the new measures are as flawed as the old
admit their difficulty while still recommending them
questions.explanation: The author concedes the measures are harder and lead to conclusions like "a slower road can be a better one", then argues that a street judged only by throughput will keep failing the people it does not count.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage's view of improvisation?
options: It is invention within shared constraints, learned by practice
It is an older form of music than composition is
It is the free expression of whatever a performer feels
It is easier to master than composing music on paper
questions.explanation: Musicians value "the ability to move fluently within" rules built through practice, not the absence of rules.

questions.stem: Why does a phrase that lands on the first beat of the cycle delight listeners?
options: It surprises them by breaking the rules of the mode
It shows that the performer had composed it in advance
It signals that the performance is about to end
They knew where it had to land and heard it get there
questions.explanation: The passage says it delights "precisely because they knew where it had to land": the pleasure comes from stretching the frame without breaking it.

questions.stem: The author compares learning improvisation to:
options: speaking fluently without consulting grammar
learning the rules of a game by reading its rule book
copying a teacher's performance note for note
memorising a written score before a concert
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the teacher makes the rules so familiar that the student stops consulting them, "much as a fluent speaker no longer consults grammar while talking."

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, composed and improvised music differ mainly in:
options: whether the choices are constrained by rules
the number of notes each performer may use
the time available for each musical choice
the expectations they share with listeners
questions.explanation: The passage ends: "What differs is the time available for the choice, not whether the choice is constrained." Both share expectations with listeners.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about:
options: how a map's purpose shapes what it shows
the techniques surveyors use to measure land
why modern maps are more accurate than older ones
the history of sea charts and lighthouses
questions.explanation: The passage argues that every useful map omits things, that what it omits reflects its maker's purpose, and that readers should ask who made a map and for what.

questions.stem: Why does the author say a map that matched the ground in every detail would be useless?
options: It would contain errors that no one could correct
It would take too long for any surveyor to draw
It would show only the features a sailor needs
It would be as large and as hard to use as the ground
questions.explanation: The first paragraph: such a map "would be as large as the ground and just as hard to use."

questions.stem: In the example of revenue maps, the author implies that the maps:
options: helped erase customary rights by recording a single owner
were more accurate than the shared customs they replaced
were drawn mainly to help sailors find their way inland
were deliberately falsified by the families who used the land
questions.explanation: Revenue maps recorded "a single owner for land that in practice was used by many families", and when read as fact "the shared uses vanished from the record". The map "helped to create" the situation.

questions.stem: What is the author's attitude to maps by the end of the passage?
options: They are less useful now than satellite images
They should not be trusted for any serious purpose
They are useful if read with their purpose in mind
They are neutral pictures of the world as it is
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the questions about who made a map "do not make a map less useful"; they let it be used for what it is good at.

questions.stem: The author's main claim is that libraries now matter chiefly because they:
options: lend more books than they did a generation ago
offer cheaper internet access than a phone does
hold rare books that cannot be found anywhere online
provide protection for attention, which has become scarce
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says access is plentiful and attention scarce, so a reading room's value lies "less in what it holds than in what it keeps out."

questions.stem: According to the passage, the prediction that libraries would fade away has proved:
options: impossible to judge, since libraries keep no records
entirely wrong, since lending of every kind has risen
only half right, since lending fell but reading rooms filled
entirely right, since few people now visit libraries
questions.explanation: The first paragraph: "The prediction has proved only half right. Libraries have lent fewer of some kinds of books, yet ... their reading rooms are fuller than ever."

questions.stem: Students queue for library seats even though they have the material at home because:
options: a quiet room of people working makes focus easier
librarians help them prepare for their examinations
the library's copies are more up to date than theirs
studying at home is forbidden before examinations
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the room "supplies a kind of shared discipline that is hard to produce alone."

questions.stem: The author would most likely criticise a library that judges its success only by:
options: the hours of quiet work it makes possible
the number of students who study there
the number of seats occupied each day
the number of books it lends each year
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says libraries "that measure their success only by the number of books lent are counting the wrong thing."

questions.stem:
The four sentences below, labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4, form a coherent paragraph when put in the right order. Decide the order and type it as a sequence of four numbers (for example, 2143).

1. The second is to remove the fear that a wrong answer will be punished.

2. Teachers who want students to ask questions must do two things.

3. Only then will students take the risk of admitting what they do not know.

4. The first is to leave silence after asking, so that students have time to think.
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 announces two things, 4 gives the first, 1 gives the second, and 3 concludes with "Only then". Order: 2413.

questions.stem:
The four sentences below, labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4, form a coherent paragraph when put in the right order. Decide the order and type it as a sequence of four numbers (for example, 2143).

1. Over time, that small difference adds up to a large one.

2. A stone dropped in a stream changes the water's path only slightly.

3. The bank on one side is worn away a little faster than the other.

4. Rivers often owe their bends to accidents of this kind.
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 starts the story, 3 states the slight difference, 1 says it adds up over time, and 4 generalises "accidents of this kind". Order: 2314.

questions.stem:
The four sentences below, labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4, form a coherent paragraph when put in the right order. Decide the order and type it as a sequence of four numbers (for example, 2143).

1. A shop that lowers its prices may win customers from its rivals.

2. In the end every shop sells as much as before, but at lower prices.

3. But its rivals are unlikely to stand still for long.

4. They cut their own prices, and the customers drift back.
questions.explanation: Sentence 1 states the first move, 3 turns with "But its rivals", 4 gives their response ("They cut"), and 2 concludes "In the end". Order: 1342.

questions.stem:
Five sentences about a topic are given below, labelled 1 to 5. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not fit and type its number.

1. Bamboo grows faster than almost any other plant.

2. Some kinds can add many centimetres to their height in a single day.

3. This speed makes bamboo a renewable material for building.

4. Pandas eat little else in the wild.

5. A grove cut for timber can be harvested again within a few years.
questions.explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 argue that bamboo's speed of growth makes it a renewable building material. Sentence 4 about pandas' diet is off the topic.

questions.stem:
Five sentences about a topic are given below, labelled 1 to 5. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not fit and type its number.

1. Proverbs survive because they are easy to remember.

2. Their rhythm and rhyme help them stick in the mind.

3. Many languages have proverbs that contradict each other.

4. Short and vivid, they can be passed on without being written down.

5. This made them useful in societies where few people could read.
questions.explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 4 and 5 explain why proverbs are memorable and so spread orally. Sentence 3 about contradictory proverbs raises a different point.

questions.stem:
The passage below is followed by four summaries. Choose the one that best captures the essence of the passage.

"A city that builds more roads to ease congestion often finds the roads filling up again within a few years. Faster travel encourages people to make trips they would not have made, to live farther from work, and to drive rather than take the bus. The new capacity is used up by the traffic it creates."
options: Faster travel always reduces the total amount of traffic.
Congestion is caused mainly by people living far from work.
New roads invite extra traffic that soon uses up the space they add.
Cities should stop building roads and invest only in buses.
questions.explanation: The passage says new capacity is "used up by the traffic it creates". It does not prescribe buses only, and long commutes are one of several effects.

questions.stem:
The passage below is followed by four summaries. Choose the one that best captures the essence of the passage.

"Museums once displayed objects with little more than a name and a date, trusting visitors to look closely. Today many exhibits surround each object with screens, sounds and explanations. These help visitors who know little, but they can also crowd out the object itself, so that people read about a painting more than they look at it."
options: Museums should go back to showing only names and dates beside objects.
Visitors today know less about art than visitors did in the past.
Screens and sounds have made museums more popular than ever before.
Modern displays inform but can pull attention from the objects.
questions.explanation: The passage weighs the benefit of explanations for beginners against the risk of crowding out the object. It does not call for a return to labels only.

questions.stem:
The passage below is followed by four summaries. Choose the one that best captures the essence of the passage.

"A company that rewards its sales staff only for the number of contracts they sign should not be surprised if many of those contracts are later cancelled. People pursue what is measured and paid for. If the quality of a sale matters, it has to be part of what is rewarded."
options: Rewards shape behaviour, so they must cover everything that matters.
Sales staff are dishonest whenever they are paid by commission.
Companies should stop measuring the work of their sales staff.
Contracts are cancelled mainly because customers change their minds.
questions.explanation: The passage argues that people chase what is rewarded, so quality must be rewarded too. It blames the incentive, not dishonest staff.

questions.stem: How many thousand units of the four factories' June output were defective in all?
questions.explanation: North 6% of 50 = 3, South 5% of 40 = 2, East 10% of 30 = 3, West 5% of 60 = 3. Total 3 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 11 thousand.

questions.stem: Which factory's output grew by the highest percentage from April to June?
options: West
South
East
North
questions.explanation: East 20 to 30 is +50%; North 40 to 50 and South 32 to 40 are each +25%; West 52 to 60 is about +15%. West has the biggest output but the smallest growth rate.

questions.stem: What was South's average monthly output over the three months, in thousand units?
West's share of the four factories' total output in June is closest to:
questions.explanation: June total = 50 + 40 + 30 + 60 = 180. West's 60 is 60/180 = one third, about 33%.

questions.stem: Which student has the highest total across the three tests?
options: Charu
Ela
Bhanu
Dev
questions.explanation: Totals: Asha 216, Bhanu 231, Charu 228, Dev 240, Ela 228. Dev's 240 is highest, even though his Reading mark is the lowest in the class.

questions.stem: What is the class average in Maths?
How many students scored more in Science than their own average across the three tests?
questions.explanation: Compare each Science mark with the student's average: Asha 64 vs 72 (no), Bhanu 76 vs 77 (no), Charu 80 vs 76 (yes), Dev 86 vs 80 (yes), Ela 82 vs 76 (yes). Three students.

questions.stem: A prize goes to every student whose total is at least 228. How many students win it?
questions.explanation: Totals of 231 (Bhanu), 228 (Charu), 240 (Dev) and 228 (Ela) qualify; Asha's 216 does not. The two totals of exactly 228 count, since the rule says at least 228.

questions.stem: Who lives on floor 1?
options: Jai
Kavya
Lal
Isha
questions.explanation: Lal, Gita and Kavya are on three consecutive floors starting on an odd floor, and Harsh is higher still, so Lal must be on 3 (Lal on 1 leaves no lower floor for Isha; Lal on 5 leaves no room above). Then Gita is on 4, Kavya on 5 and Harsh on 6. Isha's even floor below 3 is floor 2, and Jai takes floor 1. Jai is on floor 1.

questions.stem: On which floor does Gita live?
questions.explanation: Lal, Gita and Kavya are on three consecutive floors starting on an odd floor, and Harsh is higher still, so Lal must be on 3 (Lal on 1 leaves no lower floor for Isha; Lal on 5 leaves no room above). Then Gita is on 4, Kavya on 5 and Harsh on 6. Isha's even floor below 3 is floor 2, and Jai takes floor 1. Gita is on floor 4.

questions.stem: How many people live on the floors between Isha's floor and Harsh's floor?
questions.explanation: Lal, Gita and Kavya are on three consecutive floors starting on an odd floor, and Harsh is higher still, so Lal must be on 3 (Lal on 1 leaves no lower floor for Isha; Lal on 5 leaves no room above). Then Gita is on 4, Kavya on 5 and Harsh on 6. Isha's even floor below 3 is floor 2, and Jai takes floor 1. Isha is on 2 and Harsh on 6, so Lal, Gita and Kavya (floors 3, 4 and 5) are between them.

questions.stem: Who lives on the floor directly below Kavya?
options: Harsh
Isha
Lal
Gita
questions.explanation: Lal, Gita and Kavya are on three consecutive floors starting on an odd floor, and Harsh is higher still, so Lal must be on 3 (Lal on 1 leaves no lower floor for Isha; Lal on 5 leaves no room above). Then Gita is on 4, Kavya on 5 and Harsh on 6. Isha's even floor below 3 is floor 2, and Jai takes floor 1. Kavya is on floor 5 and Gita on floor 4.

Mohan

options: Pune
Agra

options: Mohan, lawyer
Omkar, chef
